sentences: After visiting the fictional country of the mountain state, English tourist the young woman is returning home to get married, but an avalanche blocks the railway line.
The stranded passengers are forced to spend the night at a hotel.

In the same predicament are the first Englishman and the second Englishman, cricket enthusiasts anxious to see the last days of a Test match in the northern city, and the old lady, a governess and music teacher.
The old lady listens to a folk singer in the street, but he is strangled by an unseen murderer.
That evening, the young woman is bothered by a loud noise from the room above hers.
It is caused by the young man, an ethnomusicologist who plays the clarinet for local folk dancers.
She attempts to get him removed from the room but fails after he confronts her.
The next morning at the railway station, the old lady drops her glasses near the young woman and her friends.
When the young woman tries to return the old lady's glasses, she is hit on the head by a large planter dropped from above.
The old lady helps her onto the train.
As she waves goodbye to her friends, the young woman faints and then comes to in a compartment with the old lady and several strangers.
Also on board are the first Englishman and the second Englishman, the young man, and lawyer the married man with his mistress, who is passing herself off as "the married man's wife".
The young woman joins the old lady in the dining car for tea.
The old lady gives a package of her favourite tea to the waiter and says she only drinks this brand.
Soon after they return to their compartment, the young woman falls asleep.
When she wakes up, the old lady has vanished.
The other passengers in the compartment, several other passengers and train staff deny ever seeing her.
The married man pretends not to remember her to avoid drawing attention to his liaison with his mistress.
The young man agrees to help the young woman search for the old lady.
Brain surgeon the doctor says the young woman may be suffering from "concussion-related hallucinations".
Fearing that any delay would make them miss the cricket match, the first Englishman and the second Englishman also claim not to remember the old lady.
Angry at her lover for his reluctance to pursue a divorce, the married man's mistress admits to seeing the old lady.
At the first stop, the doctor's patient, whose head is completely covered in bandages, is brought aboard on a stretcher and accompanied by an apparently deaf-mute nun.
A woman dressed exactly like the old lady, the impostor, appears in her place and claims to have helped the young woman after she was struck on the head.
After the married man tells his mistress his wife would never agree to a divorce, she says that the impostor was the woman she saw.
The young woman briefly doubts her own memory, but while in the dining car with the young man, she recalls having tea with the old lady and sees where the woman wrote her name on the window.
She pulls the emergency brake and faints again.

The young man still believes the young woman is hallucinating, but when one of the cooks tosses trash out the window, the young man sees a tea package wrapper briefly stick to a corridor window and recognizes the special brand the young woman told him was the old lady's favourite, convincing him of her existence.
While continuing their search, the young woman and the young man find the old lady's glasses in the baggage car.
However, they are attacked by magician the conjurer, who was in the young woman's compartment.
They lose the glasses in the struggle, and the conjurer escapes.
The young woman notices that the nun accompanying the doctor's patient is wearing high heels, and they suspect that "patient" has been replaced by the old lady.

The doctor takes them to the dining cars for a drink and accompanies them back to a compartment, where he admits that the patient is the old lady, that he is involved in the conspiracy and that they have been drugged.
However the false nun, revealed to be a British woman in costume, did not put the drug into their drinks out of loyalty to her fellow countrymen.
The young man and the young woman escape, free the old lady and replace her with the impostor.
When the train stops near the border, the doctor discovers the switch.
He has part of the train diverted onto a branch line, where soldiers wait.
The young man and the young woman inform their fellow passengers what is happening.
A uniformed soldier boards and requests that they all accompany him.
They knock him out and take his pistol.

The film is a murder mystery set at the original football stadium, the street, the district, the capital, the then home of the professional football club, one of the dominant teams in English football.
The backdrop is a friendly match between the professional football club and the amateur team, a fictitious amateur side.
One of the amateur team's players drops dead during the match and when it is revealed he has been poisoned, suspicion falls on his teammates as well as his former mistress.
The detective inspector is called in to solve the crime.
The victim has been poisoned by a powerful digitalis-based chemical.
There is evidence that he was being blackmailed.
The investigation gets complicated when the girlfriend (a prime suspect) is also murdered by the same method.
The police set a trap by putting a chemical on top of the poison, which turns the skin black after a few hours.
The player responsible is then spotted whilst playing.
In a district of the city, the victim is murdered by an unknown man, who then ransacks her house, ripping her furniture apart as if desperately searching for something.
The house remains empty for many years, until newlyweds the husband and the wife move in.
The wife soon finds herself misplacing small objects; and, before long, the husband has her believing she is losing her sanity.
The investigator, a former detective involved in the original murder investigation, begins to suspect the husband of the victim's murder.

The gas lamps in the house dim slightly, which disturbs and confuses the wife - such dimming suggests that someone elsewhere in the house has been lighting additional lamps - but when the wife asks the servants, they say that nobody else is in the house.
Unknown to everyone is that the husband has entered the upper floor from the roof and has turned on the lamps upstairs while he searches for jewels.

The sinister change in light levels, as well as unexplained noises, heighten the wife's insecurity due to the pattern of deception to which the husband subjects the wife, such as berating her for losing a brooch, which he had hidden inside his locked rolltop desk.

The investigator gets wind of the husband's plan to have the wife certified insane and institutionalised so that he can carry on with the servant girl, their promiscuous maid, and summons the wife's concerned cousin for help in getting her out of the husband's grasp.

After the husband verbally abuses the wife before leaving to attend a music hall show with the servant girl, the investigator comes to the house and reveals to the wife that the husband is really the wanted man, who has returned to the house to search for the rubies he was unable to find after murdering his aunt, the victim.
Furthermore, due to the wanted man's bigamous marriage to another woman in a distant country, his marriage to the wife is invalid.

The investigator forces open the husband's desk in search of evidence that the husband is the wanted man, but is interrupted when the wife sees the gaslight flicker shortly before the wanted man returns to the house.
The investigator confronts him with their knowledge and the wanted man mockingly opens the desk drawer which he is confident contains no evidence.
Inside is the wife's missing brooch, and she reveals that the brooch has a secret compartment in which the rubies had been hidden.
When the brooch is opened the victim's initials can be seen inside.
The wife also tells the investigator that she hid the rubies inside a vase on the mantelpiece.
The cornered wanted man attacks them both with a chair, but is knocked unconscious by the investigator.
The wanted man attempts to coerce the wife into freeing him from his restraints, but she denounces him at knifepoint before he is led away by the police.
The inspector is typing a report to his chief at police headquarters on the "amazing events" beginning on 17th August 1944, with the postman "the first to die".
We see the operating theatre and the personnel in a rural hospital.
"Two will be dead, one a murderer".
The missile offensive sends flying bombs far from the capital.
The postman reports for duty as a warden, and a "doodlebug" hits.
A wireless plays in the wreckage –an Englishwoman giving an enemy propaganda broadcast.
The postman comes into the hospital unconscious, without identification.
The surgeon commiserates with the first nurse about the nightmares she has had since the death of her mother, suggesting the work with bombing victims is a reminder.
The second nurse tells the surgeon that she has broken her engagement to the doctor, an anaesthetist.
A bomb lands, and they kiss under the watchful eye of the nursing sister.
The nursing sister runs away, hiding tears.
The first nurse recognises the postman, who reminds her of her mother.
Before surgery, the third nurse recognised the name.
The postman becomes distressed when he hears the third nurse's voice.
The doctor administers the anaesthetic.
Something is wrong.
Full oxygen is of no help.
"They neglected nothing," the inspector says.
"The postman was quite dead".
At a big staff party, a bitter nursing sister warns the doctor that the surgeon is after the second nurse.
She announces to the party that she has proof that the postman was murdered.
Leaving the party, she goes through the windy night to the operating theatre to retrieve her proof and is met by a gowned and masked figure holding a scalpel.
The second nurse finds her body.
The inspector arrives and interviews the five suspects: the doctor, the surgeon, the second nurse, the first nurse and the third nurse.
He reveals that the nursing sister was stabbed to death, then dressed in a gown and stabbed a second time.
In addition, some poison pills are missing.
The doctor shows the inspector the anaesthesia set-up.
"There was the vital evidence," the inspector recalls, "Right under my nose… It might have saved another life".
The investigation continues.
The second nurse has suspicions, but the others advise her to talk to the inspector.
She goes to bed.
The third nurse puts a shilling in the gas meter to heat a kettle.
The gas fire in the second nurse's room is on but not lit.
The first nurse calls for help but falls, dropping the second nurse downstairs headfirst.
The Inspector meets with the suspects.
He reveals that the postman recognised the voice of the third nurse's twin sister on the wireless.
The second nurse has a skull fracture.
A craniotomy is required, or she will not recover –and tell what she knows.
The inspector asks them to re-enact the operation that killed the postman.
The surgeon is not a brain surgeon, so he will assist the specialist.
When a bus crashes due to faulty steering, a passenger, the chemist (the lead actor), sustains a serious brain injury and a young girl under his care is killed.
Guilt-ridden, he attempts suicide twice during his recovery.
He starts a new job as an industrial chemist and gets a room in a hotel.
When he reluctantly accepts an invitation for a night out, he meets the young woman (the lead actress), the sister of his colleague (a supporting actor).
They begin seeing each other quite regularly.
Things reach the point that he confesses he wants to marry her, but he tells her that he wants to be sure he has fully recovered first.
The neighbour (a supporting actress), one of the other hotel residents, asks to borrow £30 from him, a rather substantial sum.
As he does not have that much on him, the chemist agrees to write her a cheque.
She is found strangled the next night.
The lover (another actor), a married businessman the neighbour had been seeing, has an alibi.
The chemist admits to have been walking in the vicinity of the murder site.
That and the recovered cheque from the crime scene and his head injury make him the prime suspect.
The police inspector (a further actor) suspects he was another of the neighbour's boyfriends and that after falling in love with the young woman, he wanted to rid himself of a possible blackmailer.

When the chemist learns that the lodger, the person who lived in the room directly below the neighbour's, had falsely told the police that the chemist was in her room every night, the chemist confronts him in his room.
The lodger brazenly admits killing the neighbour since he is confident that there is no evidence against him.
He had regularly given her money.
When the chemist made her a loan, it had given rise to the lodger's insane jealousy, with fatal results.
The chemist goes to the police, but they do not believe him.
When they come to take him into custody, the chemist flees.
He follows the lodger to the railway station and discovers from a tag on the man's luggage that he intends to flee the country by plane.
He phones the police inspector with the flight information, but when that appears to have no effect, he contemplates suicide again.
Then, a letter the neighbour had posted to the lover just before her death is found.
It incriminates the lodger, who is arrested.
The young woman finds the chemist and gives him the good news.
The writer, an American author of Western pulp novels, arrives in the British sector of the Allied-occupied city seeking the old friend, a childhood friend who has offered him a job.
However, the writer is told that the old friend was killed by a car while crossing the street.
At the old friend's funeral, the writer meets two military security men, part of the international police body: the sergeant, a fan of the writer's novels, and the major.
Afterward, the writer is asked to lecture at a book club a few days later.

He then meets a friend of the old friend's, the so-called baron, who tells the writer that he and another friend, the associate, carried the old friend to the side of the street after the accident, and that, before he died, the old friend asked them to take care of the writer and the old friend's girlfriend, the actress.
As the writer and the actress query the old friend's death, they realise that accounts differ as to whether the old friend was able to speak before his death, and how many men carried away the body.
The porter at the old friend's apartment tells them that he saw a third man helping.
He offers to give the writer more information but is murdered before they can speak again; the writer and the actress flee the scene after a mob begins to suspect him of the murder.

When the writer confronts the major and demands that the old friend's death be investigated, the major reveals that the old friend was stealing penicillin from military hospitals, diluting it, and then selling it on the black market, injuring or killing countless people.
The writer agrees to drop his investigation and leave.
An inebriated writer visits the actress and confesses his feelings for her.
A man crosses the street towards her front door, but moves away after seeing the writer at the window.
After leaving, the writer walks the streets until he notices the actress's cat and realises someone is watching from a darkened doorway.
In a momentary flash of light, the writer sees that the man is the old friend.
The writer calls out, but the old friend flees and vanishes.
The writer summons the major, who realises that the old friend has escaped through the city's sewers to the Soviet sector.
The British police exhume the old friend's coffin and discover that the body is that of a hospital orderly who had been assisting him.
The actress, who is Czech, is to be sent to the Soviet sector after the British police discover that she has a forged Austrian passport, and is questioned again by the major.
The writer goes to the so-called baron and asks to see the old friend.
The old friend and the writer meet and talk as they ride the giant Ferris wheel.
The old friend speaks cynically of the insignificance of his victims' lives and the personal gains to be earned from the city's chaos and deprivation.
The writer realises that the old friend sold the actress out to the Soviet authorities for his own benefit.
The old friend obliquely threatens the writer as he is now the only 'proof' that the old friend is alive, however the writer retorts that the authorities are aware of the false burial.
The old friend then offers the writer a chance to join in on his scheme before leaving quickly.
The major asks the writer to help arrest the old friend; he agrees provided that the major will arrange for the actress to leave the city rather than be handed over to the Soviets.
The British authorities arrange for the actress to take a train to another capital, but she spots the writer, who has come to observe her departure, at the station.
After persuading the writer to reveal the plan to capture the old friend, she leaves in order to warn him.

Exasperated, the writer decides to leave the city; on the way to the airport, the major stops at a hospital to show the writer children dying of meningitis who were treated with the old friend's diluted penicillin, which convinces him to stay and assist in capturing the old friend.
The old friend arrives at a café in the international zone to meet the writer, but the actress is able to warn him that the police are closing in.
He flees into the sewer, with the police following him underground.
The old friend shoots and kills the sergeant, but the major shoots and badly wounds the old friend.
The old friend drags himself up a cast-iron stairway to a street grating but cannot lift it.
The writer, armed with the sergeant's gun, runs after the old friend finding him beneath the grating where they stare at each other.
The major, realising the writer has chased the old friend, shouts that the writer must not take any chances and shoot on sight.
The old friend nods his head slightly at the writer.
The major follows down the tunnel as a single shot is heard.
The writer attends the old friend's second funeral at the risk of missing his flight out of the city.
He waits on the road to the cemetery to speak with the actress, but she walks past without glancing in his direction.
The widow is found murdered at her house.
As the superintendent and the inspector question her friends and neighbours, flashback scenes play out widely differing interpretations of the dead woman and her behaviour.
The neighbour tells the superintendent that the widow was a gentlewoman whereas her sister is rude and obnoxious.
According to the neighbour, the two sisters once had an argument about the widow's husband having an affair with the sister.
The sister then left after hurting the widow's feelings.
A few days later, the sister and her boyfriend, the magician, forced their way into the widow's flat.
The neighbour ran to get the help of the shopkeeper, the timid owner of a pet shop opposite the building.
The sister and the magician threatened to kill everyone and left.
This leads the superintendent to question the sister.
The sister claims that the day she visited her sister, the neighbour gave her a bad welcome.
According to the sister, the widow was a drunk, rude and not-very-pleasant-looking woman.
The sister told the widow that she went to visit the husband, however, the widow accused her and the husband of having an affair.
They argue and the sister leaves in contempt.
She admits to dating the magician and visiting the widow in his company, however, the neighbour refused to let them in.
The magician admits to meeting the widow at her workplace, where she is a fortune teller.
He, being a magician by profession, gave her a script for a mentalism act for her to go through, which she agreed to learn, but then ignored.
He visited her again two days later and the widow attempted to seduce him, throwing him out when he refused.
The day when he and the sister went to visit the widow, she treated them disrespectfully and asked them to get out.
The shopkeeper, the pet shop owner, portrays the widow in a positive light.
She once came into his shop to ask for help with her bird.
When the bird died, the shopkeeper comforted the widow and offered a parrot to replace it.
On a following day, he was politely sent away from her place due to the arrival of the sailor, a merchant sailor.
On the day the sister and the magician barged in and the neighbour asked for help, the shopkeeper claims he bravely sent both of them away.
He says that the widow had agreed to marry him the previous night before her death.
The sailor also admits to having met the widow at her fortune-telling place.
After beginning a relationship with the widow, the sailor set sail and returned after about three months.
She immediately welcomes him and they kiss.
The shopkeeper sees the kiss and immediately leaves.
On another night, the sailor sees the widow with the shopkeeper and she dismisses his concerns, angering him.
He is away for three more months of sailing.
Having promised to write to her, but not having done so, he arrives at her house, to see another man in there and sees that she is possibly a prostitute.
Furious, he refuses to listen to her explanations, manhandles her and leaves in a rage.
He says he later regretted his behaviour, blaming himself for not having written to her, which he says he is no good at.
The superintendent and the inspector return to the neighbour's house to question her some more.

In the background, the inspector can be heard questioning the boy, who mentions that he hears the words, "Merry Christmas", which were the words the widow had taught her original bird that had supposedly died thus alerting the superintendent that the shopkeeper's story contains lies.
The superintendent remarks that the shopkeeper's version of the story is the most unlikely of all.
They ask the shopkeeper to imagine a situation where the sailor could have got drunk and entered the widow's flat to kill her.

The shopkeeper agrees that it must have happened that way but when the killing happens, the superintendent switches the killer with the shopkeeper, vividly describing how a humiliated shopkeeper uncontrollably strangled the widow (shown in flashback) provoking a confession.
The superintendent and the inspector leave with a remorseful shopkeeper under arrest.
In the city an English woman asks for help from a visiting American writer to find out who has killed her brother, who was run over in a heavy nighttime fog.
Having no evidence, the police will take no action.
The writer and the English woman visit the nightclub owner's nightclub which the brother frequented, and there they learn the brother's last address.
The writer finds the brother's hotel room has been ransacked and he is knocked out by a man hiding in the room, but finds a tape recording.
Among the brother's correspondence is a letter leading the writer to an actress.
The actress is despondent over a break-up with the brother.
The actress mentions a producer with whom the brother had arranged a screen test for her.
That too appears to be a blind alley.

However, a speeding car tries to run the writer down, and he finds his own quarters ransacked, leading him to conclude he is onto something and he cancels his plans to leave the city for his home country.
He also confesses romantic feelings for the English woman.
The writer listens to the tape recording of a distraught man recounting a garage fire he was forced to set in a provincial town which killed someone called by his first name.
The writer attempts to replay it for the English woman, but accidentally erases the tape; nonetheless he remembers enough to pursue the lead.
He learns the man killed was a businessman whose partners, the producer and the second partner, relocated to the city afterwards with the widow.
The writer returns to the producer who stonewalls him, but mentions that the second partner cracked up during the war and was in a mental hospital at the time he died, two years ago.
Receiving conflicting information at the hospital, the writer sneaks in and learns the second partner is still there.

The second partner readily admits that the widow made the second partner and the producer murder her husband; however the second partner also says he is insane and cannot distinguish fact from fantasy.
The second partner slips out of the hospital, but is run down and killed by the producer's henchman.
The writer tells the English woman he believes her brother was blackmailing the producer.
The English woman believes this places the writer in danger.
Checking a bombed building for clues, the writer is knocked out by an assailant.
The English woman is visited by the nightclub owner who says she will bring her to the producer.
The nightclub owner wraps herself in a distinctive scarf last seen on the brother's killer.
It is another very foggy night, and the nightclub owner asks the English woman to walk ahead with a flashlight, intending to run her down, but the car stalls and the fog clears.
At the producer's, the English woman learns the nightclub owner is the widow and married to the producer.
The writer arrives in time to rescue the English woman.
The henchman and the producer are killed and the widow is apparently killed in a car accident, fleeing the scene.
The writer and the English woman then leave for his home country together.
A major international financier is found shot dead in the grounds of his provincial country estate.
The newspaper sends its leading investigative reporter to cover the story.
The reporter manages to get past the police cordon and speak to the inspector, the detective leading the investigation.
At the inquest, the assistant gives evidence that the financier gave him instructions to go to the port town to meet a man, the contact.
The financier said he would travel with the assistant as far as the golf course and walk back to the house for some exercise.
That was the last time the financier was seen alive.
The assistant claimed he continued on to his destination, but the police had been unable to trace the contact.
The coroner's verdict is suicide.
The reporter, however, is convinced it was murder and persuades his editor to let him pursue the story.
At first, the widow gives the reporter permission to investigate.
The assistant prepares to leave and the widow tells him they should not see each other again.
The reporter continues his investigations.
The widow changes her mind and asks her uncle to persuade the reporter to stop investigating.
The reporter says his investigation is complete.
The reporter, by now in love with the widow and aware of her husband's cruelty, visits the widow and hands over his final report.
He says he will leave it up to her whether to send the report on to his newspaper.
She does not send it.
Several weeks later, at a concert in the capital, the reporter meets the widow.
He tells her that suppressing the report has been a weight on his conscience.
She says she understands, if he believes that she and the assistant were lovers and the assistant shot her husband.
She tells him the truth: a week before her husband died, they had been due to go to the theatre, but her husband was delayed and the assistant took her to the theatre instead.
During the evening, the widow realised that the assistant was in love with her, though she felt only friendship for him.
When they returned home, the assistant kissed her and she knows her husband saw them.
She believes his jealousy drove him insane and that is why he shot himself.
The reporter is not convinced.
At a meeting with the uncle and the assistant, the reporter outlines, in detail, the circumstantial evidence that indicated the assistant murdered the financier.
The assistant then explains to him why he is completely wrong.
It was true that the financier had given the assistant instructions to meet the contact.

However, the financier also told the assistant he feared the contact would not be in the port town, and that if he was not, the assistant must continue on to a foreign capital posing as the contact to deliver an envelope.
It was also true that the financier did accompany the assistant as far as the golf course.
However, after the financier exited the car, the assistant had doubts.
He opened the envelope the financier gave him, and found money and diamonds.
He realised that the financier was framing him, and intended to ruin him.
The assistant turned the car around to have it out with the financier, only to find him lying dead on the ground.
The assistant's gun lay beside him.
Knowing he would be the obvious suspect, the assistant decided to give himself an alibi, by creating the impression that the financier did not die till much later.
He entered the house and impersonated the financier's voice so the staff would hear him talking on the phone.
He then continued on to the port town, though he knew it was a futile trip.
The reporter believes the assistant.
It is assumed that the financier killed himself with the intention of laying the blame on the assistant.

A convicted female blackmailer is found murdered in her flat and suspicion falls on three men, all of whom the police believe might have had a motive: the struggling author was involved in a relationship with the dead woman; the author's publisher, who had been blackmailed out of several thousand pounds while she was in his employ, and the playwright who knew the woman but is evasive about the exact nature of their acquaintance.
None of the three can provide a verifiable alibi for the time of the murder, so the inspector decides to shadow them in the belief that sooner or later the guilty party will betray himself.
Meanwhile, the author has fallen in love with the playwright's wife, who is tired of her loveless marriage, and the pair begin an affair.
The playwright is suffering from a heart condition and his life expectancy may be as little as a few months.
He has written an episodic radio play, "the serial", which he wants to present anonymously and he agrees to the wife's suggestion that the author should be the narrator on the broadcasts.
The wife persuades the author to go along with a plot to pass off the play as the author's own work in an attempt to boost his career.
The wife then poisons the playwright with his medications, trusting that his death will be attributed to his medical condition.

But the inspector knows about her affair with the author, and when the playwright dies, the inspector has suspicions, and the wife is horrified when he informs her that an autopsy will be carried out.
The author tells the wife that he will confess to the murder rather than see her charged, but she attempts to dissuade him.
When the autopsy results come back, they show that the playwright died of natural causes, so the couple believe that they are off the hook.
However, prior to his death, the playwright had seen newspaper reports that the author was the anonymous "writer", and was angry that the author was not denying them.
So he has set up an elaborate posthumous revenge, and, as the last episode of "the serial" is broadcast, the inspector realises that the storyline is pointing him towards the blackmailer's killer.
